{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=theoretical+frameworks+machine+agency+accountability+autonomous+systems&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Authorship responsibilities of scientists who use AI research agents.\", \"abstract\": \"The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) tools capable of performing research independently, which we call AI research agents (AIRAs) is likely to significantly impact how science is planned, performed, reviewed, evaluated, and communicated. However, the expected gains in efficiency and productivity from the deployment of AIRAs should not undermine science's epistemic and ethical values, such as accountability, transparency, reproducibility, and rigor. In this paper, we revisit the AI authorship debate in light of the reported capabilities of AIRAs and argue that these tools do not qualify for authorship because they cannot be held morally responsible for their contributions. We also reject the use of the term \\\"scientist\\\" to refer to these tools and argue that human scientists who use AIRAs have three key authorship responsibilities: (1) to carefully oversee and manage AIRAs; (2) to accurately and appropriately disclose AIRAs' contribution to research; and (3) to be accountable for research involving AIRAs by addressing questions and concerns raised by the scientific community and the public. Finally, we consider some related researcher responsibilities that are topics for future research, including the obligation to monitor, audit, and evaluate the performance of AIRAs and the obligation to address the social, economic, legal, and environmental implications of using AIRAs.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fgene.2026.1954843\", \"pmid\": \"42908681\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13683075\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fgene.2026.1954843\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13683075\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\",…

{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=automated+scientific+discovery+systems+problem+prioritization+algorithms+absence+of+objective+functions&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Hybrid artificial intelligence and quantum annealing as an optimization layer in drug discovery.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence (AI) has greatly expanded the generative capacity of drug discovery, yet the ability to translate large candidate pools into structured, resource-aware decisions remains limited. This review addresses this emerging optimization bottleneck by examining quantum annealing as a potential decision-optimization layer within hybrid computational workflows. We focus on discrete, constraint-dominated tasks-such as compound subset selection, combinatorial design, and multi-objective prioritization-that can be formulated as quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems. Rather than positioning quantum annealing as a predictive tool, we analyze its role as a complementary optimization interface integrated with AI-generated scores. We further discuss practical implementation considerations, including embedding overhead, noise, scalability, and benchmarking challenges.
